ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure there is a circle, and point Q is outside the circle. Segment QP connects from Q to point P on the circle, and the problem states that PQ is a tangent; the length of this tangent on the figure is marked as 8. Another secant starting from Q passes through the circle, first intersecting the circle at R, then intersecting at S; the external segment QR is marked as x, and the inside-the-circle segment RS is marked as 7, so the length of the whole secant QS is x+7. Then reason: By the tangent-secant theorem, the square of the tangent length equals the secant external segment multiplied by the whole secant, namely QP^2 = QR·QS. Substitute the values in the figure: 8^2 = x(x+7). So 64 = x^2 + 7x, and arranging gives x^2 + 7x - 64 = 0. Using the root formula, x = (-7 ± sqrt(7^2 + 4·64))/2 = (-7 ± sqrt305)/2. The length takes the positive value, so x = (-7 + sqrt305)/2 ≈ 5.232. Rounded to the nearest tenth, x ≈ 5.2.

method.method_draft: Read the diagram as a circle with external point Q. Segment QP is tangent to the circle at P and is labeled 8. From the same external point Q, a secant goes through the circle, meeting the near point R and far point S; the external part QR is labeled x and the inside part RS is labeled 7, so the whole secant QS is x+7. Use the tangent-secant power theorem: (QP)^2 = (QR)(QS). Set 8^2 = x(x+7), solve x^2+7x-64=0, take the positive root, and round to the nearest tenth to get x ≈ 5.2.
